t: Networks: LAN, WAN, internet, hardware and topologies
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCSE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson L16: Networks: LAN, WAN, internet, hardware and topologies.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Compare a LAN and a WAN and give examples of each. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

A network is a group of computers and devices linked by cable or wirelessly so they can share resources and communicate. A computer that is not linked to anything is called a standalone computer. A local area network (LAN) covers a small area, such as one school or office, and its hardware is usually owned by the organisation. A wide area network (WAN) covers a large geographical area and relies on telecommunications links such as fibre optic cables or satellites, often rented from other companies.
Makes sense. Keep going.

The internet is the biggest WAN of all. Organisations use networks because users can log on anywhere, share printers and files, and have their data backed up and protected centrally. Networks also have costs: hardware must be bought, a technician is needed, and viruses can spread from one computer to all the others.
Right. What else do we need to know?

The internet and the World Wide Web are not the same thing. The internet is the global network of networks: the cables, routers and connections that carry data. The World Wide Web is one service that runs on the internet. It is made up of web pages, written in HTML and joined by hyperlinks, which are stored on web servers.
Got it. Keep going.

Each site has a unique URL and pages are sent using HTTP or HTTPS. An intranet uses the same technology as the internet but is private. Only authorised users who log on with a username and password can use it, so it is useful for sharing staff documents, forms and messages. The Internet of Things (I o T) describes everyday objects, such as fitness watches, smart thermostats and video doorbells, that contain sensors and connect to the internet to send and receive data.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

Every computer on a network needs a network interface card (NIC). This circuit board lets the computer connect to the network and gives it a port for a cable. Laptops and phones have a wireless NIC instead. Network cables physically link each NIC to another device. Most are copper twisted-pair cables in categories such as CAT5e and CAT6, where CAT6 can carry data faster.
Okay. Keep going.

A switch is the central connection point in a LAN. It checks where each piece of data is going and forwards it only to the intended computer, using MAC addresses. A router connects separate networks, such as a school LAN and the internet. It reads the IP address on data and sends it along the best route to its destination. Many routers also include a firewall to filter traffic.
Go on.

A topology is the layout of a LAN. In a bus network every computer joins one backbone cable, with a terminator at each end to stop signals reflecting back. It is cheap and needs little cable, but if the backbone breaks the whole network stops, and collisions slow it down when it is busy. In a star network each computer has its own cable to a central switch (or server).
Right. Keep going.

A broken cable only affects one computer and it is easy to add more, but more cable is needed and the whole network fails if the central device fails. In a ring network each computer links to two neighbours to form a loop and data moves in one direction. There are no collisions, but one broken link stops the ring, and adding a computer means breaking the loop.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
LAN?
Local area network: a network covering a small geographical area such as one building or site, usually owned by the organisation.
WAN?
Wide area network: a network covering a large geographical area that uses telecommunications links such as fibre optic cables or satellites.
Standalone computer?
A computer that is not connected to a network, so its files and devices cannot be shared.
Internet?
The global network of networks: the hardware and connections that carry data between computers worldwide.
World Wide Web?
A collection of linked web pages stored on web servers and accessed over the internet using a browser.
Intranet?
A private network owned by an organisation that uses internet technology but can only be accessed by authorised users who log on.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

This lesson appears on almost every Unit 1 paper. Topologies are the favourite: bus, star and ring diagrams or descriptions came up in the 2019 paper, question 6 to (d), the 2022 paper, question 7, the 2023 paper, question 7 and the 2024 paper, question 6. For a bus network, name the backbone and say what a terminator does; for a disadvantage, say the whole network fails if the backbone fails. Switch and router were asked in the 2021 paper, question 6 and the 2023 paper, question 7. Keep them separate: a switch forwards data to the right computer within a LAN, a router connects networks and uses IP addresses to route data. In the 2025 paper, question 8 many candidates could not expand I o T, so learn 'Internet of Things' and have an example ready. Internet versus WWW needs both halves: network of networks versus pages accessed over it. 'Distinguish' questions need a comparison, not two separate definitions.
Let's finish with a question for the listeners. In which topology is every computer connected by its own cable to a central switch? Is it A, Bus; B, Ring; C, Star; D, Backbone?
I'll give you a few seconds.
The answer is C: Star. In a star topology each device has its own link to the central device, so one broken cable only affects one computer.
That's it for Networks: LAN, WAN, internet, hardware and topologies. Next, try the worksheet and the quiz for this lesson on the hub.
Thanks for listening. See you next time.
